sections.title: The 6 Must-Know Design Patterns — SOLID + PATTERNS: MASTER INTERVIEW Q&A
sections.body:
### 🔴 SRP Interview Questions

**Q1: How do you identify an SRP violation in existing code?**
> **✅ Answer:** "I ask: 'How many reasons could make me change this class?' More than one = violation. Red flags I look for: (1) Class name with AND — `UserAuthAndEmailService`; (2) Methods from completely different domains in one class — `save_to_db()` + `send_email()` + `generate_pdf()` in one class; (3) The class has 500+ lines; (4) When testing, you need to set up unrelated infrastructure — to test an email, you need a DB running. In a recent code review, I found `OrderManager` doing: order creation, tax calculation, PDF invoice generation, email sending, and DB persistence — 5 separate responsibilities in 800 lines. We split it into 5 classes. Each became 100-150 lines. Test coverage went from 40% to 95% because each class was independently testable."

**Q2: Is SRP about having only one METHOD per class?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Absolutely not. SRP is about ONE REASON TO CHANGE, not one method. A class can have 20 methods as long as they all serve the same single responsibility. `UserRepository` can have: `save()`, `find_by_id()`, `find_by_email()`, `find_all()`, `delete()`, `update()` — 6 methods, but all serve ONE responsibility: data persistence for Users. The litmus test is not method count but actor count — how many different stakeholders (business team, DBA, email team) would request changes to this class? More than one stakeholder = more than one responsibility."

### 🟠 OCP Interview Questions

**Q3: How does OCP relate to the use of Abstract Classes and Interfaces?**
> **✅ Answer:** "ABCs and interfaces ARE the mechanism for implementing OCP. The ABC defines the CLOSED part — the stable interface that never changes. Concrete subclasses are the OPEN part — you add new behaviour by creating new subclasses without touching the ABC or any existing concrete class. Example: `PaymentGateway(ABC)` with `charge()` and `refund()` is closed. Adding Razorpay, Stripe, PayPal = three new concrete classes. The `CheckoutService` that depends on `PaymentGateway` NEVER changes. In our fintech project, we added 4 new payment gateways over 2 years — zero changes to `CheckoutService`."

**Q4: Can you violate OCP even when using ABCs?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Yes — if the ABC itself changes, you violate OCP. If I add `partial_refund()` to `PaymentGateway(ABC)`, now ALL existing implementations (`RazorpayGateway`, `StripeGateway`, `PayPalGateway`) must be modified. That's modifying existing code. Better approach: create a new `PartialRefundable(ABC)` interface and only implement it in gateways that support it. The existing `PaymentGateway` stays closed. Another common violation: using `isinstance()` checks in business code — `if isinstance(payment, Razorpay): ...` — this forces you to modify the business code every time a new payment type is added."

### 🟡 LSP Interview Questions

**Q5: What is the practical test for LSP compliance?**
> **✅ Answer:** "The substitution test: take ALL unit tests written for the parent class and run them against the child class. If any test fails for the child, LSP is violated. Three specific rules the child must follow: (1) **Preconditions** — child cannot STRENGTHEN preconditions (if parent accepts any positive number, child cannot require it to be > 100); (2) **Postconditions** — child cannot WEAKEN postconditions (if parent guarantees sorted output, child cannot return unsorted); (3) **Invariants** — child must maintain the same class invariants as parent. I use this in code reviews: if a PR introduces a subclass and the reviewer can't run existing parent tests against it, the PR is flagged."

### 🔵 ISP Interview Questions

**Q6: How does ISP prevent the 'interface pollution' problem?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Interface pollution is when implementing a class forces you to implement methods that are irrelevant to it — usually with `raise NotImplementedError`. This is a code smell that signals ISP violation. ISP prevents it by breaking fat interfaces into role-specific ones. The benefit: when you see `class Robot(Workable, Rechargeable)`, you IMMEDIATELY know what a Robot can do. You don't need to read 20 methods wondering which ones are relevant. Practically: I model interfaces around what CLIENTS need, not what servers provide. `OrderService` needs `find_by_id()` and `save()` — it doesn't need `bulk_delete()` or `get_audit_log()`. So `OrderService` gets an `OrderReader` + `OrderWriter` interface, not the full `OrderRepository`."

### 🟣 DIP Interview Questions

**Q7: What is Dependency Injection and how does it implement DIP?**
> **✅ Answer:** "DIP says 'depend on abstractions'. Dependency Injection (DI) is the TECHNIQUE to achieve it. Instead of a class creating its own dependencies (`self.db = MySQLDatabase()`), dependencies are PASSED IN from outside (`def __init__(self, db: Database)`). Three forms: (1) **Constructor injection** — passed in `__init__` (best — dependencies visible and required); (2) **Setter injection** — set after construction via methods; (3) **Interface injection** — less common in Python. DI containers (like Python's `dependency-injector` library) automate the wiring. Benefits I've experienced: in a 50-service microservices project, DI meant every service could be tested in complete isolation. Build time for test suite dropped from 15 minutes to 2 minutes because no real services needed to start up."

### 🎯 Design Pattern Interview Questions

**Q8: What is the difference between Singleton and a global variable?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Both provide global access, but Singleton is superior in 4 ways: (1) **Lazy initialization** — created only when first needed, not at program start; (2) **Controlled instantiation** — the class itself controls when/how the single instance is created; (3) **Subclassing** — can extend a Singleton class; (4) **Thread safety** — can implement double-checked locking; a global variable has none of this. The real danger of both is hidden coupling — any code anywhere can access the Singleton, making dependencies invisible. In modern design, I prefer Dependency Injection over Singleton even for 'single-instance' objects — you still create one instance, but inject it explicitly so dependencies are transparent."

**Q9: When would you choose Factory Method over Direct Instantiation?**
> **✅ Answer:** "I use Factory when: (1) The exact type of object to create isn't known until runtime — `NotificationFactory.create(channel_type)`; (2) Creating an object requires complex setup logic that shouldn't be in `__init__`; (3) I want to centralize creation logic so changes to how objects are created are made in ONE place; (4) I need to return cached/pooled instances instead of always creating new ones. Direct instantiation when: the type is always known, creation is simple, and I don't anticipate variations. In a payment system, `PaymentGateway.create(country)` returns different gateway implementations per country — the factory knows India uses Razorpay, USA uses Stripe, EU uses Adyen. Business code never needs to know."

**Q10: How is the Decorator Pattern different from Python's @decorator syntax?**
> **✅ Answer:** "They share the name and concept but are distinct. Python's `@decorator` syntax is a language feature — it wraps FUNCTIONS at definition time using higher-order functions. The Decorator DESIGN PATTERN is an OOP pattern — it wraps OBJECTS at runtime using class composition. Both add behaviour without modifying the original. The design pattern is more powerful for objects: you can stack multiple decorators on one object at runtime, each adding different behaviour. Example: `LoggingDecorator(EncryptionDecorator(CompressionDecorator(FileProcessor())))` — 4 levels of wrapping at runtime. You can add/remove decorators dynamically. Python's `@decorator` syntax is static (applied at definition). I often implement the Decorator Pattern using Python's class system, not the `@decorator` syntax — they're two different tools."

**Q11: Explain Observer Pattern vs direct method calls.**
> **✅ Answer:** "Direct method calls create tight coupling: `Order` must know about `EmailService`, `InventoryService`, `Analytics`, `FraudDetection`. Adding a new reaction to order placement means modifying `Order`. With Observer: `Order` knows nothing about its observers. It just emits events. New reactions (new observers) are added without touching `Order`. The coupling direction is inverted — observers depend on Order's events, not Order on observers. This is the Open/Closed Principle applied to event-driven architecture. In our e-commerce platform, when we added fraud detection (6th observer on order events), the `Order` class had zero changes. The fraud team wrote their observer, registered it at startup, done."

**Q12: When should you NOT use the Repository Pattern?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Repository adds a layer of abstraction — that abstraction has a cost. Don't use it when: (1) The application is simple CRUD with no complex business logic — adding Repository is over-engineering; (2) You're building a script or one-time tool — abstraction adds complexity with no benefit; (3) You're using an ORM like Django's ORM which already IS a repository (adding another layer doubles the indirection); (4) The data model maps 1:1 to the business model with no transformations. Use Repository when: complex business logic needs testing without a DB; when you might switch databases; when multiple data sources need to be unified behind one interface. In a Django project, I use the ORM directly for simple CRUD views but wrap complex queries in repository classes for service-layer code."

sections.title: The 6 Must-Know Design Patterns — ADVANCED PATTERNS: COMPLETE INTERVIEW Q&A
sections.body:
### 🟤 Adapter Q&A

**Q1. What is the difference between Adapter and Facade?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Both wrap other objects, but for different reasons. **Adapter** makes two INCOMPATIBLE interfaces work together — it converts one interface to another. The wrapping is about translation, not simplification. `LegacyPaymentAdapter` translates paise→rupees, status codes→strings. **Facade** simplifies a COMPLEX SUBSYSTEM by providing a single unified interface. It doesn't translate — it hides and orchestrates. `OrderFacade` hides 6 subsystems behind `place_order()`. Quick test: Are the interfaces compatible but the system complex? → Facade. Are the interfaces incompatible? → Adapter. In practice: I use Adapter when integrating third-party SDKs or legacy systems into our modern codebase. I use Facade when a complex microservice flow needs to be exposed as a single clean API."

**Q2. When would you use a Class Adapter vs Object Adapter?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Object Adapter (composition) is almost always preferred. It wraps the adaptee via `self._adaptee = adaptee`. Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance: `class MyAdapter(TargetInterface, Adaptee)`. Object Adapter advantages: works even when you can't subclass the adaptee (final classes, built-ins); can adapt multiple adaptees in one adapter; follows composition over inheritance. Class Adapter advantages: can override adaptee methods directly; slightly less code. In Python, I always use Object Adapter — Python's multiple inheritance can create MRO issues, and composition is cleaner."

### 🟦 Facade Q&A

**Q3. Does Facade prevent clients from accessing subsystems directly?**
> **✅ Answer:** "No — Facade doesn't restrict access, it simplifies it. Clients CAN still access subsystems directly if they need fine-grained control. Facade is not an access barrier (that's Proxy). It's a convenience layer. In practice: most clients use the Facade for common operations. Power users or advanced features might bypass the Facade and call specific subsystems. Example: `OrderFacade.place_order()` for normal checkout, but `PaymentSubsystem.authorize()` directly for a custom partial-payment feature. The Facade doesn't prevent this — it just means you don't HAVE to know all subsystems for the common case."

### 🟧 Proxy Q&A

**Q4. What is the difference between Proxy and Decorator Pattern?**
> **✅ Answer:** "They look identical in code structure — both wrap an object with the same interface. The difference is INTENT: **Decorator** adds NEW behaviour to an object — it ENRICHES the object. You stack Decorators to compose features: `LoggingDecorator(CachingDecorator(Processor))`. **Proxy** controls ACCESS to an object — it doesn't add new features. A Virtual Proxy delays creation. A Protection Proxy checks permissions. A Caching Proxy returns cached results (the real object would return the same anyway). Key: Decorator clients know they're using a decorator chain. Proxy clients ideally don't know they're using a proxy — they think they're talking to the real object. If I'm enriching = Decorator. If I'm controlling access = Proxy."

### 🟥 Command Q&A

**Q5. How does Command Pattern enable undo/redo functionality?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Each Command stores enough information to REVERSE itself. Execute stores the current state; Undo restores it. Implementation: maintain two stacks — history (executed commands) and redo (undone commands). `execute(cmd)` → runs command, pushes to history, clears redo stack. `undo()` → pops from history, calls `cmd.undo()`, pushes to redo. `redo()` → pops from redo, calls `cmd.execute()`, pushes to history. The key: every command must be self-contained with all data needed to undo. `DeleteCommand` stores the deleted text so it can be restored. `ReplaceCommand` stores the entire original content. For complex operations, `MacroCommand` undoes all sub-commands in reverse order in one step. Used in: every text editor, Photoshop, Git revert."

### 🟩 Chain of Responsibility Q&A

**Q6. How is Chain of Responsibility different from Strategy?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Superficially similar — both have a family of handlers. Key differences: **Strategy** has ONE handler selected and used. You explicitly choose which strategy to apply. **Chain of Responsibility** passes the request through MULTIPLE handlers until one (or all) handles it. The sender doesn't choose — the chain decides. Also: in Strategy, all strategies can handle any request. In CoR, each handler has a specific capability range — if it can't handle, it passes on. When to use which: 'I need to process data with algorithm X' → Strategy. 'I need to find the right handler for this request from a chain of options' → CoR. Example: middleware stack in a web framework is pure CoR — each middleware either handles the request (auth error) or passes it to the next."

### 🟪 State Q&A

**Q7. How does State Pattern eliminate complex conditionals?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Without State Pattern, every method in the Context class has a giant if/elif chain:
> ```python
> def pay(self, txn):
>     if self.state == 'draft':
>         raise Error('Not confirmed')
>     elif self.state == 'confirmed':
>         self._process_payment(txn)
>     elif self.state == 'processing':
>         raise Error('Already paid')
>     elif self.state == 'cancelled':
>         raise Error('Order cancelled')
> # × 8 methods = 32+ conditional branches!
> ```
> With State Pattern: each state class handles one specific situation. `ConfirmedState.pay()` just processes payment — it doesn't check other states. Adding a new state (`BackorderedState`) = new class + no changes to existing states or Context. The if/else explosion is eliminated. In a payment system with 7 states and 8 actions, this reduced 56 conditional branches to 7 focused state classes."

sections.title: The 6 Must-Know Design Patterns — DDD COMPLETE INTERVIEW Q&A
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between an Entity and a Value Object?**
> **✅ Answer:** "The fundamental difference is **identity**. An Entity has a unique identity that persists through time — `Customer` with ID `C001` is the same customer whether their address is Mumbai or Delhi, whether they're 25 or 35. Two entities with different IDs are different objects even if every attribute matches. A Value Object is defined entirely by its VALUE — `Money(1500, 'INR')` and another `Money(1500, 'INR')` are identical and interchangeable. Value Objects are immutable — you don't change them, you replace them. `Money(1500)` → `Money(1500) + Money(500)` returns a NEW `Money(2000)`. Three quick tests for Value Object: (1) Can I replace one with another of same value? (2) Is it immutable? (3) Does it have no lifecycle of its own? If yes to all three → Value Object. In our banking system, `Account` is an Entity, `Money` is a Value Object, `TransactionAmount` is a Value Object, `AccountHolder` is an Entity."

**Q2. What is an Aggregate Root and why does it matter?**
> **✅ Answer:** "An Aggregate is a cluster of objects (Entities + Value Objects) that are treated as a UNIT for data changes. The Aggregate Root is the ONLY entry point into the cluster — external code can ONLY reference the root, never the internal objects directly. Why it matters: (1) **Consistency boundary** — the root ensures all invariants within the aggregate are maintained. `Order` ensures you can't add items after confirmation, can't pay incorrect amount; (2) **Transaction boundary** — one aggregate = one transaction. Never update two aggregates in one transaction; (3) **Repository boundary** — you only have repositories for roots, not for internal entities. The design rule: 'if you're holding a reference to an OrderLine directly, something is wrong — get it through Order.' In our e-commerce system: `Order → OrderLines (Value Objects)` is one aggregate. `Product → (stock, pricing)` is another. They coordinate through Domain Services."

**Q3. What is a Domain Event and when should you use them?**
> **✅ Answer:** "A Domain Event represents something SIGNIFICANT that happened in the domain — past tense, immutable fact: `OrderPlaced`, `PaymentReceived`, `StockDepleted`. Use them when: (1) Multiple parts of the system need to react to something but shouldn't be tightly coupled; (2) You want eventual consistency between bounded contexts; (3) You need an audit trail of everything that happened; (4) You want to implement undo/replay. The pattern: Aggregates RECORD events internally during operations. After the transaction commits successfully, the Application Layer DISPATCHES the events. This two-phase approach prevents events from being dispatched for failed transactions. In practice: `Order.confirm()` records `OrderConfirmed` event internally. `OrderService` dispatches it after `order_repo.save()` succeeds. Email service, inventory service, analytics — all react to the dispatched event without `Order` knowing about them."

**Q4. What is the difference between a Domain Service and an Application Service?**
> **✅ Answer:** "**Domain Service**: contains BUSINESS LOGIC that doesn't naturally fit in one Entity or Value Object. It operates on domain objects, speaks the ubiquitous language, has no knowledge of infrastructure. `OrderFulfillmentService.place_order()` is Domain Service — it coordinates Order + Product aggregates using business rules. **Application Service**: orchestrates use cases, coordinates Domain Services and Repositories, handles cross-cutting concerns (transactions, security, logging). It's the entry point from the outside world (REST controllers call Application Services). It knows about infrastructure but delegates business logic to the domain. Rule: if it contains an `if` based on a business rule → Domain Service. If it just coordinates and delegates → Application Service. Common mistake: putting business logic in Application Services — this is an anemic domain model."

**Q5. What is Ubiquitous Language and why is it important?**
> **✅ Answer:** "Ubiquitous Language is the SHARED vocabulary between developers and domain experts (business team) that's used consistently in conversation, documentation, AND CODE. The goal: eliminate translation overhead. When a business analyst says 'when a customer places an order, we allocate inventory' — the code should have `customer.place_order()` and `inventory.allocate()`, not `UserTransaction.create()` and `StockManager.decrementUnits()`. Why important: (1) Reduces bugs caused by translation errors between business intent and code; (2) Makes code readable to domain experts (they can validate logic); (3) When requirements change, the changed business vocabulary immediately maps to code changes. I enforce this in code reviews — if a business term appears in requirements but doesn't appear in the code, that's a smell. In a fintech project, renaming `Transaction` to `Transfer` and `Movement` to `LedgerEntry` (business terms) eliminated a whole category of misunderstandings between our team and the finance department."

**Q6. What is a Bounded Context and why can't one model rule the entire system?**
> **✅ Answer:** "A Bounded Context is an explicit boundary within which a particular Domain Model applies. The same word can mean different things in different contexts — 'Customer' in Sales context (lead, prospect, conversion funnel) vs 'Customer' in Billing context (invoice, payment history) vs 'Customer' in Shipping context (delivery address, preferences). Trying to build ONE Customer object that satisfies all contexts creates a bloated, conflicted model. Instead: each Bounded Context has its own Customer model with only what IT needs. Contexts communicate through APIs or events, with explicit mapping (Context Map) between them. In a large e-commerce platform: `Order Context`, `Inventory Context`, `Payment Context`, `Shipping Context`, `Notification Context` — each has its own models. `Product` in Order context = name + price. `Product` in Inventory context = SKU + stock levels + warehouse location. They're deliberately separate."

**Q7. When should you NOT use DDD?**
> **✅ Answer:** "DDD adds significant complexity — it's only worth it for complex business domains. Don't use DDD when: (1) **CRUD-heavy systems** — if your app is mostly 'create form, save to DB, show list', DDD is massive overkill. Active Record pattern is fine; (2) **Simple domains** — if business logic is minimal (a blog, a todo app), DDD ceremonies add no value; (3) **Time-constrained projects** — DDD requires deep domain analysis and collaboration with business experts; (4) **Technical problems** — DDD is for business domain complexity, not technical complexity (a compiler, an OS kernel). Use DDD when: complex business rules that keep changing; multiple teams working on different parts of a large system; when business experts and developers need to collaborate deeply. The heuristic I use: 'Could a business analyst read my domain model and validate it?' If yes, DDD is adding value. A financial trading system, hospital management, insurance underwriting — these scream DDD."
